statement: The CRFSC is an introductory course designed for novice users of restricted firearms and people who want to acquire them.
The Canadian Firearms Program (CFP) is managed by the RCMP, working with provincial chief firearms officers to administer the Firearms Act.
CFP activities include licensing all firearm owners and businesses, delivering the safety courses, public education on storage/transport/use, and import/export controls.
Licensing and registration information is kept in the Canadian Firearms Information System, a national CFP database to which law enforcement has some access.
All firearms safety course instructors and examiners must be recognized by the chief firearms officer of the province or territory where the course is taken.
The CRFSC includes classroom lessons, manual study, and written and practical exams, but no live-fire exercises.
When you hear of a firearm accident, at least one of the vital four ACTS rules was broken.
Vital rule T: treat every firearm as if it were loaded (assume it is potentially dangerous).
Vital rule P: always point the firearm in the safest available direction and never at yourself or anyone else.
Vital rule T: keep your finger off the trigger and out of the trigger guard except when firing.
Vital rule O: only hand over or accept a firearm when its action is open and it is unloaded.
PROVE sequence: Point in safest direction, Remove all cartridges, Open action and check chamber(s), Verify feeding path, Examine bore for obstructions.
The last PROVE step is to examine the bore to make sure it is free of obstructions.
A valid licence holder must notify the Firearms Program before moving so that an authorization to transport can be issued for restricted firearms.
A possession-only licence (POL) holder may borrow firearms of the same class they may possess; a PAL holder may borrow, buy, inherit or otherwise acquire firearms of that class.
Hunting with a restricted firearm is prohibited in Canada.
Municipal bylaws (noise, nuisance, zoning) may prohibit discharging a firearm anywhere within municipal limits.
Beyond the law, keep an inventory of your firearms with photos and manuals in a safe place to help describe a lost or stolen firearm.
Pointing a firearm, loaded or unloaded, at another person without lawful excuse is a Criminal Code offence punishable by up to five years if prosecuted as indictable.
FFFFg (pulvérin) is the finest black powder and is used only for priming flintlock pans, never as a propellant.
FFFg is the most common black powder grade and is used in almost all muzzleloading revolvers and pistols.
The finer the black powder granules, the higher the pressure when fired.
Black powder can be ignited by a spark, static electricity, heat, friction or a sudden shock.
Black powder should be stored in a safe, cool, dry place in its original container.
Aged black powder that clumps and forms white crystals is very dangerous and should be immersed in water immediately.
Smokeless powder must never be used in a muzzleloader; only black powder or black powder substitutes such as Pyrodex.
Glowing embers can remain in the bore after firing a black powder firearm, creating an explosion risk if reloaded immediately.
A Minié ball is a conical bullet with a hollow base that expands to prevent gas escaping during firing.
In a percussion muzzleloader, ignition comes from the hammer striking a percussion cap; in a flintlock, from the flint striking the frizzen.
To make sure a muzzleloader is not primed: point safely, finger off trigger, check hammer not cocked, check for cap or priming powder, remove it.
Marking the ramrod at the empty-bore depth shows whether a muzzleloader is loaded.
Always use a volumetric measure to pour powder into the muzzle, never directly from the container, flask or horn.
Under safe storage rules, a black powder firearm is considered loaded when there is powder in the barrel, and must not be stored with powder in it.
Clean a black powder firearm after every shooting session with a black powder solvent or hot soapy water, because black powder is very corrosive.
In a black powder revolver, grease over each ball prevents chain firing of all chambers.
Treat a muzzleloader misfire as a possible hangfire: keep it pointed safely for at least 60 seconds.
Rifling is a series of spiral grooves inside the barrel; the metal between the grooves is called lands.
Rifling makes the bullet spin as it leaves the barrel, giving it stability in flight.
Calibre is the bore diameter, in thousandths of an inch (land to land) or in millimetres (groove to groove).
Imperial calibre is usually measured land to land, metric dimensions groove to groove.
The most important thing is to match the cartridge designation on the head stamp with the markings stamped on the barrel or slide.
If a firearm has no markings (or markings may be wrong due to modification), have a qualified person check it and measure the chamber.
Never accept or use reloaded cartridges unless you are certain they were made and reloaded correctly; improper loads can make the firearm explode.
The two main types of modern cartridges are rimfire and centrefire, named for where the primer is located.
In rimfire ammunition, the priming compound is inside the rim; the firing pin crushes the soft rim to ignite it.
In centrefire ammunition, the primer is at the centre of the case head and is used in more powerful, larger calibres.
.22 Magnum cartridges are not interchangeable with other .22 rimfire cartridges.
Dry-firing a rimfire firearm (firing sequence with no cartridge in the chamber) can damage it.
A handgun cartridge has four components: bullet (hits target), powder (propels), case (holds components), primer (ignites charge).
A bullet fully covered at the tip is jacketed (ball); one with exposed lead at the tip is semi-jacketed.
Cartridges with different designations are not interchangeable (e.g., .38 S&W, .38 Special, .38 Super Auto).
The head stamp shows the cartridge designation, calibre, manufacturer and regular/magnum quality; reading it is the only way to be sure the cartridge matches.
Some ammunition, such as rimfire cartridges, may have no designation; check the box and have it verified if in doubt.
Handguns can fire bullets more than two kilometres; shooters must know their projectile's danger range.
Trajectory is the curved path of a projectile, affected by gravity, air resistance, velocity and mass; it crosses the line of sight twice.
A hangfire is a delayed ignition; removing the cartridge too soon can make the case burst and cause injury.
A squib load fires with little noise or recoil and may leave the bullet stuck in the barrel; firing again can burst the barrel.
After a misfire, hangfire or squib, wait 60 seconds pointed safely, then open the action, remove the ammunition and PROVE the firearm safe, checking the barrel for obstruction.
Restricted firearm ammunition must be stored away from the firearm unless stored in a securely locked container or a vault/safe/room built or modified for restricted firearms.
In a residence, restricted firearm ammunition must not be displayed with the firearm.
Store ammunition in a cool, dry place, ideally in a ventilated container; a non-ventilated container can create an explosion hazard in a fire.
Natural Resources Canada allows a reasonable quantity of sporting ammunition for personal use, not for resale.
The safest way to transport ammunition is in its original container; carry only ammunition suited to the firearm you are using.
The two main handgun action types are the revolver (cylinder) action and the semi-automatic action.
A revolver action has several chambers in a rotating cylinder, each holding one cartridge.
A semi-automatic action extracts and ejects the empty case and chambers another cartridge with each trigger pull.
A break (hinge) action opens near the breech and is usually found on single- or double-barrel firearms.
Single action: the trigger only releases a cocked hammer.
Double action cocks and fires with one continuous trigger pull and can also fire in single action; double-action-only cannot fire in single action.
Mechanical safeties can fail; a sudden shock may fire the gun even with the safety on, so safe handling is the most important safety.
Safeties interrupt the firing sequence by blocking the trigger, sear, hammer or firing pin.
Manual safeties (slide, lever, frame, safety catch) can be put on and off; built-in safeties include decocking buttons, trigger safeties, magazine disconnects and grip safeties.
The magazine disconnect prevents firing when the magazine is removed.
The grip safety, usually on semi-automatic pistols, disengages when the gun is gripped in firing position.
A decocking button safely lowers the hammer on single/double-action pistols; double-action-only pistols have none.
A hammer block (drop safety) keeps the firing pin from striking the primer if the hammer is hit; older revolvers may lack one.
A half-cock position is not necessarily a safety; check the owner's manual.
To lower a cocked single-action hammer: firm grip with strong hand, weak-hand thumb fully on hammer, press trigger and ease hammer forward, releasing trigger once clear.
With an internal hammer (striker), it is hard to see whether it is cocked, so extra caution is needed; all external-hammer safety procedures apply.
PROVE steps: Point, Remove, Observe (open action, check chamber), Verify feed path, Examine bore.
When unloading, remove a detachable magazine first so a semi-automatic does not chamber another cartridge.
A PROVEd firearm stays unloaded and safe only while the person who PROVEd it keeps direct control.
When loading, keep the safety on (if applicable) until ready to fire, and load only when you intend to use it where legal and safe.
The owner's manual is the best source for detailed loading and unloading of a specific firearm; general steps don't replace it.
In a revolver, only one chamber aligns with the barrel when firing; cylinders rotate clockwise or counter-clockwise depending on the maker.
Most single-action revolvers have fixed cylinders loaded one cartridge at a time through a loading gate, usually on the right side.
With a single-action revolver, the hammer must be cocked manually for each shot; the trigger only releases the hammer.
Unloading a fixed-cylinder single-action revolver: if the cylinder won't rotate with the gate open, put the safety on and place the hammer at half-cock.
In a fixed-cylinder revolver, use the ejector rod under the barrel, pushed front to back, with the chamber aligned with the loading gate.
Let ejected cartridges/cases fall on the bench or floor and don't pick them up until all unloading steps are completed.
Most revolvers have no safety, though some do; check the owner's manual or a qualified gunsmith.
When loading, select cartridges by matching the firearm's marking with the cartridge head stamp.
Unloading a swing-out cylinder revolver: operate the cylinder release, swing out the cylinder, point muzzle slightly up, use ejector rod.
Pulling a double-action revolver trigger fully back rotates the cylinder to align a cartridge and cocks and releases the hammer.
When loading a double-action swing-out revolver, keep the hammer fully down if possible and close the cylinder by locking the action firmly.
Break-top revolvers work like other revolvers but the action tips up or down rather than swinging sideways.
A semi-automatic uses part of the energy of the expanding powder gases to extract the empty case and chamber a new cartridge from the magazine.
In single/double-action semi-autos the hammer stays cocked after each shot (lighter trigger); in double-action-only it returns forward.
Unloading a semi-automatic pistol: remove the magazine first, then pull the slide fully back without covering the ejection port, then lock the slide back.
Magazine release buttons are in different places (behind trigger, bottom of grip, elsewhere) depending on make and model.
Direct control means the firearm is in sight and/or within arm's reach of the shooter.
Loading a semi-auto: set the firearm down pointed safely with action open to fill the magazine, insert it until it locks, then pull the slide fully back and release to chamber a round.
Magazine capacity for semi-automatic handguns is limited by regulation to 10 cartridges.
Shooting glasses should be made of impact-resistant glass or polycarbonate and have side shields.
Eye injuries while shooting can be caused by ejected cases, case fragments and other debris.
For maximum hearing protection, wear earplugs together with earmuffs.
Disposable foam or wax earplugs can be used only once.
If you fall while holding a firearm, first control the direction the muzzle is pointing.
Button your collar and sleeves so hot ejected cases cannot get inside and startle you.
Marksmanship depends on grip, stance, aiming, trigger control, breath control and follow-through.
With a two-hand grip on a semi-automatic pistol, keep the weak-hand thumb away from behind the slide to avoid injury from slide recoil.
Hold a handgun with about the same pressure used to hold a hammer.
In the two-hand standing position, face the target squarely, feet shoulder-width apart, knees straight but not locked, arms extended with elbows locked.
In the one-hand standing position, turn the body about 45 degrees from the target and lock the elbow and wrist of the shooting arm.
Aim with the dominant eye, ideally with both eyes open; with a scope or red dot, keep your eyes on the target and raise the handgun until the sight comes between eye and target.
Sight alignment is lining up the front and rear sights on the target, which creates the sight picture.
The shot should be fired during the natural pause (about 2.5 seconds) after exhaling.
To lengthen the natural respiratory pause: breathe in deeply, exhale forcefully, breathe in deeply again, then let the air out naturally.
Good trigger control means squeezing slowly and progressively, without jerking or anticipating the shot.
Follow-through means keeping the sight picture and firing position after the shot.
Range commands vary by sport, range and jurisdiction; if in doubt, ask the range safety officer.
The range safety officer is ultimately responsible for the safety of all range users and must be obeyed at all times.
At the range, the action must be open at all times except when firing, and firearms are loaded only on the safety officer's order.
Firearms may be handled, loaded and fired only at the firing line, and only after the safety officer gives the order to load.
On 'cease fire': stop firing, unload, open the action, set the firearm down pointing safely downrange, and step back behind the cease-fire line.
During a cease fire, nobody may handle firearms or ammunition or return to the firing line until the officer gives further orders.
The safety officer inspects every firearm (actions open, no cartridges in chambers or magazines) before anyone crosses the firing line.
In an emergency, anyone may call a cease fire.
Direct control means the firearm is within the shooter's sight and/or within arm's length.
Minors and guests without a valid firearms licence must be under direct and immediate supervision at all times when shooting.
Shooters using semi-automatics should position themselves so ejected cases don't hit others; black-powder shooters should position so smoke isn't blown onto others.
Before leaving the range, with the officer's permission: pick up cases and targets, put back range equipment, and sign out in the log.
Unacceptable targets include those that can cause ricochets, glass or fragmenting materials, other people's targets and targets not directly in front of your position.
A handgun may be discharged only where it is legal, such as ranges approved by the Chief Firearms Officer; hunting with a handgun is prohibited.
Even minor repairs should be done by qualified people; the average user should only do basic cleaning and lubrication.
Rust from moisture and excessive build-up of residue can cause excessive pressure and damage the barrel, so firearms should be cleaned regularly.
Old military ammunition may be corrosive; if you use corrosive ammunition, clean the firearm immediately after use.
Whenever possible, clean the barrel from the breech toward the muzzle; if cleaning from the muzzle, avoid rubbing the rod against the muzzle to protect the rifling.
In the cleaning method, the solvent-soaked brush is passed through the bore first, then solvent patch, then dry patches until clean, then a lightly oiled patch.
Before using the firearm again after storage, run a dry patch through the bore and chambers to remove oil, since oil or dirt can raise pressure and burst the barrel.
While cleaning, keep ammunition away and avoid distractions; never clean a firearm while doing something else.
After cleaning a firearm for storage, avoid touching metal parts with bare skin because acids in sweat can cause rust.
Keep ammunition clean and dry, away from heat and vibration, and never wipe it with an oily cloth since primers react badly to penetrating oils.
Individuals may generally own restricted firearms for a lawful profession, target shooting or competition, collecting, or in very rare cases self-protection.
A handgun that is not prohibited is a restricted firearm.
A non-prohibited semi-automatic centrefire firearm with a barrel shorter than 470 mm (18.5 in) is restricted.
A firearm designed or adapted to fire when reduced by folding or telescoping to an overall length under 660 mm (26 in) is restricted.
Handguns with a barrel of 105 mm (4 1/8 in) or less, or designed to fire .25 or .32 calibre, are prohibited, except those used in ISSF competitions prescribed by regulation.
Handguns designed or adapted to fire .25 or .32 calibre cartridges are prohibited (with the ISSF competition exception).
Automatic firearms are prohibited; prohibited firearms generally cannot be acquired by individuals.
A device designed to muffle or stop the sound of a firearm (silencer) is a prohibited device.

To store a restricted firearm: unloaded, and either locked with a secure locking device inside a locked container/room not easily broken into, or kept in a vault, safe or room specially built for restricted firearms.
A restricted firearm stored in a vault, safe or room specially built for restricted firearms and kept locked does not also need a locking device.
A restricted firearm may only be stored at the address shown on its registration documents.
Storing ammunition in an unventilated container can create an explosion hazard in a fire.
To display a restricted firearm in a home: unloaded, disabled by a secure locking device, securely attached to a non-portable structure, and not displayed with or near ammunition it can fire.
When displayed away from its registered address, a restricted firearm may be detached so someone can handle it under the direct supervision of the person displaying it.
Transporting a restricted firearm between places requires an authorization to transport, obtained from the Chief Firearms Officer.

To transport a restricted firearm: unloaded, disabled by a secure locking device, and in a locked opaque container that cannot be easily broken or accidentally opened; a padlocked heavy-duty soft case can qualify.
A locked container with a restricted firearm may be left in an unattended vehicle's locked trunk; if there is no trunk, the vehicle must be locked and the container not visible from outside.
Removing the firing pin or another part of a restricted or prohibited handgun does not make it legally deactivated or safe for transport.
Pointing a firearm, loaded or not, at another person without lawful excuse is an offence; as an indictable offence it carries up to five years in prison.
Contravening the storage, display, transport and handling regulations is, on indictment, punishable by up to two years for a first offence and five years for a subsequent offence.
Only hand over or accept a firearm when its action is open and it is unloaded.
The PROVE steps are: Point safely, Remove all cartridges, Observe the chambers (open action), Verify the feeding path, Examine the bore.
A person transferring a firearm must require the recipient to show a licence authorizing acquisition and possession of that class of firearm, and be satisfied it does.
The transferor must have no reason to believe the recipient has a mental illness threatening public safety or is impaired by alcohol or drugs.
The transferor must inform a chief firearms officer of the transfer and obtain authorization.
The transferor must give the chief firearms officer both parties' names, addresses and licence numbers, and the class of firearm transferred.
For restricted firearms, the recipient must tell the chief firearms officer why the firearm is needed (e.g., protection of life, target practice or competition, or a collection).

A collector acquiring a restricted firearm must give the CFO information on knowledge of its features, written consent to reasonable periodic inspections, and understanding of safe storage requirements.
Before authorizing a transfer, the CFO must determine whether it could endanger others' safety; if authorized, both parties get the same transfer authorization number.
For a transfer completed by telephone, the transfer number serves as confirmation and as a temporary registration certificate until the new certificate arrives by mail.
